title: Dual-metric decomposition: availability leakage versus valid-time version contamination on amended clauses
research_question: On amended legal text, do availability leakage (retrieved evidence not yet public at the target date) and valid-time version contamination (retrieved passage not in force at the target date) produce the same rates and the same system rankings, or do they decompose into distinct failure modes with different base rates?
hypothesis: Availability leakage and valid-time version contamination measure different failure modes with different base rates: on amended legal clauses, contamination is dominated by superseded versions and is substantially larger than leakage, the two metrics rank retrieval configurations differently, and the 10.8% financial leakage rate is not a valid prior for the legal version-contamination rate.
proposed_method: Augment each clause version with two date attributes: its validity interval (in force from/to) and its availability date (when the text entered the public record or the corpus snapshot). For every retrieved passage, compute a four-way label combining in-force status at the target date (valid time) with public availability at the target date (transaction time). Run the standard retriever set on the Stage-0 query set, then compute both metrics from the identical frozen rankings, decompose contamination into superseded and not-yet-in-force components, and compare system orderings under each metric. Use the oracle valid-time gate headroom to set the Stage-0 threshold instead of importing the financial leakage prior.
baselines: Published three-signal hybrid with decay (strongest directly comparable)
Recency-only ranker (isolates the too-old failure direction)
Oracle availability filter and oracle valid-time gate separately, to show the ceiling for each metric independently
datasets: The curated clause version chains from Stage 0, augmented with two dates per version: a validity interval (in force from/to) and an availability date (when the text entered the public record)
Required subset: chains where availability and validity dates differ, which are the informative cases for separating the metrics

Optional comparison arm: a static regulatory corpus with documents but no version relations, where version contamination is undefined and only leakage-style measures apply, to show the metrics are not interchangeable
Not used: financial filings and ESG disclosures, whose availability regimes differ from legislative publication
workloads: Queries whose target date precedes the availability of the latest version (leakage-prone)
Queries targeting a superseded version's validity window (contamination-prone, superseded direction)
Queries whose target date lies between availability and entry into force, if such gaps exist (the informative overlap case)
Near-duplicate version pairs, where version competition rather than availability is the failure channel
Deep chains, where repeated supersession should accumulate the superseded-direction error
hardware: CPU-only: indexing and embedding a few hundred clause versions with BM25 and BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5, plus rule-based metric computation. No GPU, no reader LLM, no external API.
metrics: Availability leakage rate - fraction of retrieved passages not yet public at the target date
Version contamination rate - fraction of retrieved passages not in force at the target date

Decomposition into four cells per retrieved passage: in force and available; not in force but available (superseded); in force but not yet available (edge case); not in force and not yet available (not-yet-in-force)
Rank agreement (Kendall tau) between system orderings induced by the two metrics, with bootstrap intervals
Distribution of the gap between availability date and validity start date per version
Metadata coverage: fraction of versions with verifiable availability and validity dates
Contamination of each retriever minus contamination under the oracle valid-time gate (headroom), for threshold setting
ablations: Availability definition: official publication date vs entry into force vs first appearance in the snapshot, to test sensitivity of the leakage rate
Chain depth and age gap, since superseded-direction errors should grow with chain depth
With and without near-duplicate version pairs to test whether version competition drives contamination beyond availability effects
Target-date granularity, since day-level as-of dates should sharply separate the two metrics
controls: Both metrics computed from the identical frozen per-query rankings
Per-version validity and availability dates verified by hand with provenance recorded
Same candidate pool, k and chunking across retrievers
Per-stratum reporting with confidence intervals and sample sizes
Strict and lenient definitions of both violations reported
Threshold decisions for the broader programme taken from the oracle-gate headroom, not from either extrinsic prior
confounders_addressed: The two metrics may be near-identical if availability and validity dates coincide for most items - addressed by reporting the date difference distribution and by analysing cases where they diverge
Contamination could be inflated by the corpus containing only current versions - addressed by requiring superseded versions to be present and reporting per-version availability
Reader noise is irrelevant here because both metrics are computed from retrieval outputs only
Query-stratum composition could drive divergence - addressed by computing both metrics per stratum
Availability dates may be missing for many versions - addressed by reporting coverage and restricting the leakage metric to chains with verifiable availability dates rather than imputing
expected_outcomes: The two metrics have materially different base rates and different system rankings. Contamination is expected to be substantially larger than leakage and dominated by the superseded direction, while leakage is small and concentrated on not-yet-in-force versions; the recency-only ranker should show near-zero leakage on older queries but high contamination by selecting latest versions; rank agreement between the two metrics is expected to be low. This decomposition also yields the independently measured contamination baseline that the Stage-0 stop/go threshold requires.
failure_conditions: The two metrics produce statistically indistinguishable rates and rank systems identically - the 10.8% prior would then transfer and the dual-metric framing collapses to one metric
Availability dates cannot be recovered for enough versions, so leakage cannot be computed on the legal corpus and the comparison is impossible
Contamination turns out to be a strict subset of leakage on this corpus, meaning no superseded-direction failures occur - the amended-clause premise weakens sharply
Divergence exists but is driven entirely by a handful of chains with anomalous metadata - the result is a metadata artifact rather than a metric distinction
reproducibility_notes: No execution spec is attached: no public implementation of a clause-versioned legal retrieval benchmark exists, and the adjacent RMA repository is an interactive notebook over a static, non-versioned corpus requiring third-party PDFs and an API key, with no JSON metrics output. The study is CPU-only and rule-based, so it is cheap to replicate; release the chain metadata (validity intervals, availability dates, provenance for each), the query set with strata, every frozen per-query ranking, the four-way labelling code, and the strict and lenient violation definitions, together with the date-gap distribution used to judge whether the two metrics can diverge on this corpus.
